content.thinking:
I'm planning to write the whole file carefully in one pass without testing in between, designing a whimsical low-poly gnome about 1.15m tall with a gadget backpack. I want to keep the API usage conservative to avoid crashes, relying on builders, joints, lathes, and extrusions while making sure every import actually gets used.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton: hips as the root joint, a short spine chain rising to the chest, then a neck and head joint, working out how chain parenting and tip naming should connect so the head ends up correctly oriented above the neck.

Rather than wrestle with chain nuances for the spine, I'll just use simple parented joints (spine1, spine2) with "spine" roles, then build the body as sweeps bound rigidly to those bones. I'll keep everything in absolute model-space coordinates with explicit bone bindings to avoid orientation confusion, facing +Z with left as +X, and I'm now working out proportions for a total figure height of 1.15 units.

For the legs, I'm setting hip, knee, and ankle joint positions, then using a three-point chain per leg (hip-knee-ankle) parented to the hips, swept with tapering radii to form the trousers, with left/right sides distinguished by x-position.

For the feet, I'll place boot geometry at the ankle tip and skip separate toe joints to keep things simple, treating the ankle as the foot's tip bone.

Now I'm positioning the arms in a slight A-pose, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints for each side and starting a chain for the left arm.

For hands, I'll keep it simple with a palm sphere plus a thumb and finger capsules rigidly attached to the wrist bone rather than creating full digit joints. Then for the head, I'm setting the head joint and a slightly offset sphere for flat-shaded geometry, and starting to work out the facial features.

Adding facial details...

Also planning the jaw joint and lower beard bone structure for the chin, then starting the torso sweep path with varying radii from hips to chest.

Working out spine joint positions: hips, spine1, spine2, neck, and head, each with specific coordinates to shape the gnome's pot-bellied torso and build up toward the head sphere.

Adding shoulder pads where arms attach, then checking total height—head plus hat brim plus cone tip lands near 1.4, a bit tall, so I'll shorten the hat to around 1.3. For clothing I'm thinking a mottled green tunic for the torso, with a belt ring sweep around the waist at y 0.50.

Working out the belt as a lathed shape—inner and outer radii near 0.14-0.155 fit the torso's curve at that height, with an 8-sided circumscribed polygon approximation checking out against the target radius. Settling on belt radii around 0.15 with a smoothed 12-segment lathe.

Now adding a brass buckle box at the front, then planning a leather apron as an extruded trapezoid shape positioned against the torso's belly surface, making sure the thickness direction and outline orientation align correctly with the body's front-facing Z axis.

Checking the apron bottom near the hips against the legs — it floats about 10cm forward, which looks unnatural as cloth. I'll adjust the outline range from y=0.42 to 0.68 so the gap near the torso front is mostly hidden by the belly bulge, skipping a tilt or drape sweep since that's too risky to implement reliably.

Now moving on to accessories: attaching an apron with box-shaped tool pockets holding a screwdriver, wrench, and pliers sticking out, plus a backpack frame rigged to the spine bones with a leather box body, copper tubing frame, and strapped gadgets like a telescope, gear crank, brass steam pipes, spinning propeller, and a glowing lantern.

More gadget ideas: a kettle pot, coiled springs, toothed gear disks, a rolled umbrella, a spinning radar antenna, a giant wind-up key, an oil can, a rolled blueprint scroll, and hanging wrenches — with hinge joints for the propeller, crank, lid, and antenna dish. Now I'm working out the backpack's static attachment to the spine bone and defining the body box's position coordinates.

Working through the pack lid geometry and its hinge joint placement at the top-back edge, figuring out how the hinge's local axis orientation should align given the parent bone's default direction.

Now I'm setting up leather grain paint colors for the painted parts, noting that flat low-poly geometry will use ngon sweeps, and sketching a small helper function to streamline part creation with consistent flat shading and positioning options.

Then I'm defining helper utilities for rotating parts in model space and building boxes, cylinders, and spheres with arbitrary axis alignment, plus a rod helper for connecting two points with a specified radius and bone binding.

I'm now working out how to build a gear shape, outlining a polygon with teeth using an extrude function, orienting it so the flat face points along a chosen direction, and planning how to flip orientation for gears facing the opposite way.

For the eyes I'm planning white sphere parts with pupils, plus tinkerer-style goggles on the hat band using lathe tubes and glowing glass, and a brass monocle made from a low-segment torus with a pale blue glowing lens circle facing forward.

Now I'm sketching the facial features: bushy white eyebrow capsules, a round red nose, small flat pink cheeks, a hidden mouth box replaced by a small dark red smile capsule, and a curling white moustache built from a catmull spline path with tapering radii. I'm also placing a flattened, slightly widened head sphere as the base for the beard region.

Working through the 3D math now to position the nose and eyes correctly on the head sphere's curved surface, adjusting z-depth so they sit just proud of the face rather than embedded in it.

For the hat, I'm sketching a curved cone shape with a swept path that bends backward and droops near the tip, tapering the radius from wide at the base to a point, giving it a classic floppy wizard-hat silhouette.

Now I'm figuring out the hat's coloring with bold red striped with a lighter orange-red tone, and designing a lathed brim profile with a slightly upturned edge where it meets the head.

I'm checking the hat placement against the head geometry—making sure the brim sits just above the eyebrows without blocking the eyes, and sizing the cone base so it nestles naturally on top of the skull.

I'm repositioning the facial features to fix the collision—lowering the eyes slightly, adjusting the brow line, and raising the brim—then working out where the goggles sit on the front of the hat, using a torus pair plus a wraparound strap band at the correct cone radius.

Now I'm adding details: a leather studded band, a small bell at the hat tip, pointy spike ears built off the head bone, and starting on white hair tufts and a large beard.

For the beard, I'm shaping a flattened base sphere at the chin and attaching 7 downward-angled spike locks with varying lengths, giving them a white-to-grey gradient paint and attaching to the jaw bone so they hang naturally from the chin down.

I'm then placing the jaw joint parented to the head, adding a dark mouth box and a small pink lower lip capsule, and finishing with a hidden neck capsule beneath the beard connecting the head to the body.

For the collar, I'm shaping an orange tinker scarf as a lathe ring around the neck joint, skipping hanging tails for simplicity but considering a strip extrude for a back-left drape. Then I move to the arms, defining tapered green sleeve segments and cuffs using lathe or cone shapes oriented along the tilted arm direction.

Now I'm working out the hand and fingers: placing a skin-colored sphere for the palm at the wrist offset along the arm direction, then adding three small capsule fingers positioned with lateral offsets computed via a cross product between the arm direction and the up vector to get a proper perpendicular spread.

Still defining arm and finger geometry...

Computing the exact wrist and wrench coordinates so the rod runs vertically from the floor up through the gnome's hand...

Still defining wrench outline polygon...

Now I'm working out the left hand lantern: hanging from the wrist with a glass body, glow, brass cap, and bottom plate, positioned below the hand with floor clearance maintained. I'm also sketching the color palette for trousers, tunic, hat, beard, and skin tones.

Settling on blue trousers, brown boots, green tunic with an orange scarf, brass and copper accents, and a warm yellow glow color, then laying out the leg structure with symmetric hip, knee, and ankle joints for a straight standing pose.

Working out boot geometry...

Checking the boot cuff against the leg radius at that height looks right as a flared cuff, so I'll add knee patches in tan and sort out the sweep taper radii for the trouser leg. I'm also considering whether to add a decal emblem on the tunic or apron using an SVG patch.

For decals I'll keep things minimal: a gauge dial face texture for the pack's pressure gauge, and a blueprint scroll texture placed as a plane facing backward, both just simple colored SVGs rather than logos. I'm also thinking about flaring the tunic hem into a skirt using a lathed frustum shape.

For the tunic skirt I'm working out a lathe outline that flares from the hips down to cover the leg tops, adding a thin trim ring in yellow for a hem stripe, and checking that it doesn't collide awkwardly with the apron geometry layered in front.

Shaping the bib outline as a trapezoid with smoothed corners, then adding shoulder straps as rod-like capsules running from the bib top over the shoulders to the back, rigged to the spine bone.

Next I'm adding apron pockets as small darker-leather boxes with stitched edges, and tools sticking out of them—a screwdriver with a steel shaft and red handle, plus pliers poking out alongside it.

Then I'm placing crossed pliers with orange handles in another pocket, a tape measure cylinder in the center pocket, a hammer hanging at the hip, and a flap pouch on the opposite side, before working out the backpack's placement and dimensions so it sits flush against the torso's back without clipping through it.

Now I'm adding decorative gears on the pack's back face, and I need to figure out the correct hinge axis orientation so the gear bone rotates about the world Z axis rather than its own local X — meaning I need to orient the joint's local X to align with world Z.

Working out the dir/up combinations for each joint so the hinge axis lands on the right world axis: gears and cranks need rotation about Z (dir Y, up X), while propellers need rotation about Y (dir X, up Z). Now I'm naming the actual joints -- packLid hinge, gearA, and more to follow.

Now I'm laying out the frame geometry: copper vertical rods flanking the pack at x ±0.17/0.185, horizontal crossbars top and bottom, with poles extending upward to mount gadgets, then placing a telescope strapped horizontally across the top of the pack.

Still designing telescope segments... Then I'm planning a propeller mast rod rising from the lid's top center.

Mirroring the blade outline for the second propeller blade and adding a hub sphere, then moving on to the radar dish mounted on a mast with a parabolic bowl shape oriented upward and forward.

I'm also planning steam pipes curving along the pack's side, a pressure gauge with a brass dial facing backward, a steam valve wheel with spokes, and gears to start the next mechanical section.

Now I'm positioning two meshing gears on the back face, copper gearA and brass gearB, checking their spacing matches the sum of their radii so teeth appear to interlock properly, plus adding a crank handle nearby.

Finishing the crank arm and knob geometry, then adding a rolled blueprint scroll tube with ribbon bands and end caps near the pack's side, before moving on to a lantern piece at the bottom of the pack.

Now thinking about hanging items beneath the pack: a copper pot dangling at the bottom with clearance from the floor, a tin mug with a torus handle, and a coiled spring made from a spiral sweep.

Checking for gear collisions, I decide to reorient the spring horizontally instead, placing it along the x-axis near the bottom corner to avoid overlapping with the gears above.

Lowering the spring slightly fixes the clearance issue. Now I'm working out the shoulder straps for the pack, figuring out a curved path from the top front of the pack over the shoulders down to under the arms, checking it against the torso's surface radius so the strap hugs the body properly.

I'm adding a crossing chest strap and small shoulder pad spheres, accepting there's some risk of straps floating slightly off the torso surface but deciding it's acceptable. Next I'm moving on to designing a pair of goggles mounted on the hat using torus shapes.

Now I'm figuring out the lens placement and glow effect, tracing the cone's path length to determine where the lenses should sit along the curved surface near the top of the head.

I'm also sizing the goggle torus and band width, positioning the hat band at the right height with inner and outer radii that match the hat's curve, then moving on to the eye details with small white spheres for the eye whites.

Now I'm working out the iris, highlight, and brow placement, then considering a brass monocle ring around the left eye with maybe a hanging chain, plus a glowing blue lens, before confirming the eye z-position relative to the head sphere's radius.

Calculating where the eye sphere and monocle torus sit relative to the head's curved surface, so they protrude just enough. I'm also considering the head's geometry and shading, adding pink cheek spheres, and thinking about whether to add white sideburn tufts near the ears.

Now I'm checking the overall part count stays under the limit, and carefully building out a limited color palette (skin tones, nose highlights, beard, hat reds, eye details) to keep distinct colors around 35 and under the 64-color cap.

Rounding out the palette with red, teal, and black for about 35 colors total, which feels right. I'm planning paint treatments like mottling the tunic fabric, adding grain texture to the leather pack, and gradient shading for skin and beard, while sketching out SVG textures for a gauge dial with ticks and needle plus a blueprint pattern.

I'm now working out placement for a second sticker decal, a schematic/blueprint patch, deciding it should sit on the pack's back face since the front and sides are taken up by the scroll and telescope -- figuring out the exact coordinates within that back panel alongside the gauge.

Checking the gauge, two gears, and sticker positions on the back face for overlaps, then thinking about whether to add buckled straps or pipes, and considering merging small bolt/stud spheres into a single part for efficiency.

Now I'm planning the pack body structure: corner reinforcement strips, front and back straps with brass buckles, and side pouches with flaps, plus the lid dimensions.

For the lid, I'm deciding between a simple box or a curved cylindrical cap shape, adding a brass trim strip and latch detail, then placing a hinge joint connecting the lid to the pack frame. I'm also figuring out where the propeller mast should attach—deciding it belongs on the frame's spine rather than the lid since the lid needs to open, and sketching out the vertical frame rods' positions and height range.

Now I'm working through collision issues between the frame rods, side pouches, and the scroll object, repositioning them so nothing overlaps—shifting the scroll outward past the rods and planning small leather strap details near the frame.

On the right side I'm sorting out overlap between the crank mechanism and the pipe routing, adjusting their heights and depths so the crank arm and pipes don't intersect, then planning how the pipe should run from the pack outward.

I'm defining a curved pipe path with copper band details and a valve wheel torus, plus thinking about adding whimsical steam puff effects at the nozzle end, though I'm hesitant about the extra complexity.

Now I'm placing a crank mechanism at the lower right with an axle, and sketching out an upper frame cage structure with vertical rods, trying to work out how it avoids colliding with the lid and mast while keeping the geometry simple.

Checking whether the hat tip overlaps the pack region given their coordinates—seems fine since the propeller sits below the hat tip's height. I'm also verifying the crank axle placement on the pack's right side to make sure it doesn't clash with other elements.

Now I'm checking the left side for collisions between the pack and the skirt: the pack's back edge at its lower boundary slightly overlaps the skirt's back curve near the hips, so I'm shifting the pack upward to a higher center position with its lid resting just above that to clear the conflict.

Positioning the remaining frame rods, top bar, mast, propeller, and satellite dish, then placing the telescope on the lid clear of the frame and a scroll piece on the left side below the top.

Checking that arms, shoulders, and the backpack don't collide, and that the head, beard, hat, and pack lid stay clear of each other near the back of the skeleton.

Now I'm starting to define the joint hierarchy, beginning with the hips as root and the spine joints above it.

Continuing up through spine2, neck, head, and jaw, I'm setting positions, parent relationships, and orientation directions — making sure the jaw's rotation axis will produce a natural downward hinge motion. I'm noting that arm and leg chains branch from spine2 and hips respectively, and the pack lid attaches to spine2 as a hinge joint.

Now I'm adding the mechanical parts — gears, crank, propeller, and dish — all parented to spine2 as hinge joints, bringing the total joint count to roughly 24. I'm double-checking the arm chain's shoulder position relative to spine2, confirming leg placement near the hip joint stays within the skirt geometry, and sketching the torso sweep path through a few key points along the spine.

Now I'm checking the torso's radius profile and cap shape — the round cap at the chest top is pushing the dome too high, overlapping into the head and beard area, so I'm trimming the path endpoint down to around y=0.67 so the shoulders land cleanly at y=0.68 without colliding with the neck.

I'm sketching the bone assignments: spine bones for the torso sweep, a neck capsule with rounded caps running from y=0.72 to 0.82, and hip/spine1 bones for the skirt, apron, and belt pieces. I'm defining helper functions to build these geometry pieces with explicit color and bone options...

Defining more geometry helpers...

I'll skip the scarf tails since they'd overlap awkwardly with the beard, and decide the beard will naturally obscure much of the torso and apron top anyway. I'm shortening the beard length so the apron bib still peeks through below it.

For whimsical details, I'm adding a tiny mushroom and feather tucked into the hat band, plus a small wind-up toy robot perched on the shoulder with a box body, antenna, and glowing eye. Now I'm starting to lay out the actual geometry code, beginning with the skin-toned head sphere.

Still writing character geometry...

I should lift the hat slightly, placing the brim at y 1.005 with the band at y 1.04. Then I'm positioning goggles above the band around y 1.075-1.09 with a torus ring and glass circle, making sure their size and placement don't collide with the band geometry.

Adding goggle details now...

I'm plotting the hat path with a curved cone shape ending in a pointed tip, topped with a small yellow pompom sphere, giving the gnome a total height around 1.28m including hat — reasonable scale for a gnome figure.

Now I'm sketching SVG textures for a gauge face and decal: a circular dial with a cream background, dark circular border, and a green arc indicator.

Writing gauge SVG...

I'm also designing a sticker texture with a dark blue rectangle and a gear-like decoration, then placing both as small plane decals on the model using directional offsets so they face outward correctly.

Adding the brass ring torus and verifying gear thickness placement, then writing a gear-generation helper function with alternating radius points around each tooth.

Still writing gear logic...

Still defining gear sizing and joint placements...

Now I'm setting up the propeller joint position and orientation, then sketching the blade outline shape using coordinate pairs along its length and thickness.

I'm defining the mast as a steel rod and the frame as copper rods with corner spheres connecting the structure.

Now placing the lid and telescope assembly: a tapered lid supports a multi-section telescope tube with brass and copper sections of decreasing radius, plus a mounting band ring where sections meet.

I'm positioning the eyepiece at the back end with a smaller iron radius, and the objective lens at the front end with a larger iron radius and a glowing lens circle facing outward. Then I'm adding strap boxes and a hinge rod along the back top of the pack to connect the lid.

Below that I'm placing a copper pot with a lid and handle under the pack, plus a steel mug with a torus handle, rope rods connecting to the pack bottom, and checking that nothing dips below ground level. I'm also setting up a wrench and lantern for the hands, and starting on belt tools like a hammer on the left side.

For the hammer, I'm positioning its leather handle rod hanging from the belt loop with the iron head pointed downward near the left leg, keeping it outside the leg geometry. Then I'm adding a flattened leather pouch with a flap on the right hip.

I was considering adding a wind-up key somewhere on the pack, but after testing several placements (back, sides, near the pipe) everything collides with existing elements like the scroll and gears, so I'm skipping the key entirely. Now I'm moving on to think about placing a small robot toy on the left shoulder.

Working out robot proportions and placement...

Now I'm figuring out the arm geometry for holding objects, placing shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints and computing the hand direction vector so the palm sits naturally at the end of the wrist.

The lantern bottom sits near the thigh clearance, so that should be fine, and the glow body already handles the flame light inside the frame. Now I'm positioning the right wrench: computing the palm offset from the wrist joint to get the grip point, then setting the wrench's rod to extend down and touch the floor at y=0.

I'm placing the wrench head geometry and handle grip, with a red-banded section partway up the rod, then starting to wrap finger capsules around the rod to simulate the hand gripping it.

Still working out hand geometry...

I'll accept the fingers passing beside the gripped rod as visually close enough, with the palm sphere sized at .042 radius, then move to the wrist cuff as a small trim cylinder and sleeve taper with decreasing radii toward the wrist.

Loosening the sleeve radii slightly and adding small elbow and knee patches with leather and tan materials for visual texture, though I'll skip the stitching details since they're too fiddly to justify the complexity.

For the leg chain, I'm mapping the three named points—hip, knee, ankle—into two spans plus a tip joint at the ankle, which becomes the boot's bone anchor. I'm also adding a toe joint parented to the ankle for the foot geometry.

Working out the boot's shape now: a sole box extending roughly from the heel to the toe, with a curled spike toe cap attached as a separate rigid part on the toe bone.

Now sketching the shaft and cuff of the boot as cylinders at the ankle, plus a small brass buckle strap at the front, before moving on to defining the torso apron and skirt as a lathe shape with its own outline profile.

Still writing shape definitions...

Checking the apron placement relative to the belt front — since the belt outer edge sits at .18 and the apron spans .165-.179, they should overlap correctly with the belt visually crossing over the apron. Tracing the torso's front curve confirms the front surface at y.55 lands around .165, which lines up with the apron edge touching it properly.

Now I'm sizing the neck scarf: the initial outline is too small and gets hidden inside the torso's dome at that height, so I'm enlarging the scarf radius to .13 so it clears the torso surface, then adding a knot sphere and hanging tails as separate extrusions positioned near the front of the neck.

I'm checking the vertical gap between the scarf top and head bottom, confirming the beard will cover any visible neck capsule, then moving to finalize the head details -- jaw, lower lip, chin shaping, and a beard base sphere positioned against the jawline.

Adding beard spike geometry...

Skipping the mouth and letting the jawline carry the beard shape instead. For the moustache I'm defining a mirrored curved path per side with tapering radii from the nose area outward and downward, colored white against the bone head, with the nose sized and positioned above it. Now I'm setting up the eye loop with white eyeballs positioned symmetrically.

Working out iris...

Computing the brow capsule endpoints against the head's curved surface, then adding flat cheek details positioned similarly against the surface geometry.

For the monocle, I'm placing a brass torus frame on the left side with a pale glass circle disc facing forward, giving it a slight glow; the connecting chain would be covered by the beard so I'm skipping it to save detail. Moving on to hat decoration next.

Now I'm planning rivet placement on the pack's back face and lid edges, laying out a perimeter pattern of small brass spheres spaced along the top, bottom, and side edges while skipping corners, all merged into one geometry attached to the spine bone.

I'm also adding front strap and buckle decoration on the pack's back, placing leather straps with brass buckle accents, but checking that the strap positions don't collide with the gear shapes already placed nearby.

That texture mapping should work fine with the box geometry's UVs, and the component count is landing around 250 which feels right. I'll add a stitching strip on the lid and rising steam puff spheres near the pipe nozzle, working out their positions relative to the lid and telescope geometry.

Now I'm adjusting the pipe path so it doesn't collide with the telescope or frame rods, shifting the z-coordinates back and recalculating the waypoints up to the nozzle end where the steam puffs will sit, while nudging the frame rod position to keep a safe gap from the pipe.

I'm also repositioning the dish to the top of the left mast rod, adding a propeller at center, and placing a top crossbar between the frame rods. Now I'm defining the valve wheel on the pipe as a small copper torus rotated to face along the X-axis.

Adding pipe bands...

Now I'm setting up the telescope dish geometry: joint placement, mast rod positioning, and lathe outline for the bowl shape facing upward.

The dish gets a forward tilt via its axis vector, with a feed rod extending from the joint and capped with a sphere tip in steel. I'm checking the bowl's outline points don't cross, then considering whether to add extra pack accessories like crates or wind chimes but deciding to keep it minimal.

For the backpack gadgets, I'm adding a flagpole rod extending upward from the frame, with a teal pennant triangle attached that waves behind it, working out the cross product to orient the pennant's thickness correctly along the x-axis so it's visible.

I'm also considering swapping out the mug for a glowing jar instead—a translucent cylinder with a teal glow, brass lid, and handle, positioned where the mug currently sits on the pack.

Now I'm checking the rig structure: whether jaw bones should hide when open, confirming the neck joint attaches as a child of spine2, and making sure the rig-building function returns the root correctly at the end. I'm also double-checking imports to avoid unused references—THREE, createBuilder, rng, polyline, catmull, spiral, the paint helpers like mottle/stripes/grain/gradient, plus the Joint type and PartOptions typing—so everything stays crash-safe and properly typed.

Setting up imports and initializing the gnome tinkerer builder...

Still defining the skeleton joints...

Adding pinstripe texture to the trousers, then moving to arm chains with shoulder/elbow/wrist joints parented to spine2, sleeve sweeps, shoulder pad spheres, and wrist-tip hand bones.

Writing arm geometry code...

Still placing hand details and tool assignments — lantern for left hand, wrench for right. Now I'm adding an elbow leather patch positioned on the outside back of the elbow, scaled flat to hug the joint, before moving into the torso and lantern geometry code.

Computing the left palm position from wrist and direction vectors, then placing the lantern there with a brass handle rod running up to a grip point, a glowing lamp body box, and a small cone-topped cylinder for the lantern's cap.

I'm adding a bottom brass plate, four iron corner rods, and a brass top ring rotated to face upward, then moving on to compute the right wrist's wrench position using similar directional math.

Now I'm laying out the apron pockets and tools—leather pocket boxes with trim, plus a screwdriver with a steel shaft and red handle, sized to fit within the pocket bounds.

Adding the pencil, pliers with diverging copper handles, and a cylindrical measuring tape, positioning each tool within the left and right pockets and a small center pocket.

Now I'm assembling the full file, making sure part options and typed outline arrays (using tuple annotations for the lathe outline) don't trigger type errors, and double-checking skirt and glow handling for flat parts.

For the beard, I'm building a gradient paint and generating a fan of small spike parts jutting from the jaw with slight randomized length and position variation per spike index, while checking the direction vector sign is correct.

Adding second beard row...

Now I'm adding side locks of hair as small spikes, and deciding to use smooth:false across my helper functions for a consistent low-poly faceted look on torso sweeps and chain elements too. Time to write the actual code.

Defining the pack parts...

Adding brass trim and checking lid dimensions against torso bounds, then deciding to attach the telescope and straps to the lid bone while keeping the dish and gauge on spine2. Starting to lay out the telescope's rod sections along the x-axis...

Now adding leather straps with buckles, a glowing glass lens between the objective and eyepiece rods, and double-checking the sweep and spike geometry calls for crashes.

Checking that all the extrude outlines—blade, apron, scarf tail, pennant, wrench—are valid convex polygons with at least three non-intersecting points before verifying the thickness arguments.

I'm making sure thickness is specified for extrusion, confirming lathe segment counts, verifying gear tooth outlines stay non-self-intersecting, and working out the spiral's center, radius, axis, and pitch for the right-hand helix geometry.

I'm checking the sweep along the spiral path with small radius and few sides for a bone-like spine, confirming the `along` callback typing works despite returning a Part, verifying joint and chain parameter types, and handling the nullable result from merging geometries before constructing the cylinder.

Still working through geometry types... I'm confirming cylinder direction vectors, fill/color typing, left-right naming conventions, and the tapered sweep radii for the hat with flat-to-point end caps, then moving on to positioning the toe joints relative to the ankle.

Now I'm cataloging the painted parts across the whole character—tunic, trousers, skin with mottled texture, hat, leather, and beard spikes—making sure paint colors don't get double-counted against flat colors. Then I'm shifting to building out the robot's spine, body box, and head box with their positions and colors.

Adding glowing eyes, antenna with a red sphere tip, arm and leg rods, and foot boxes, while double-checking the shoulder pad height clears the robot body's base—then finishing off the hat feather details before writing everything out.
